title: Private Equity Acquisition of Gastroenterology Practices and Colonoscopy Price and Quality
author: Daniel R. Arnold · Brent D. Fulton · Ola A. Abdelhadi · Arjun Teotia · Richard M. Scheffler

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source examines private-equity acquisition of gastroenterology practices, not legal AI capabilities, verification, selective deployment, or work redesign. It therefore provides no relevant evidence for assessing the cluster’s proposition.

st.t: Healthcare ownership: Financial gains do not prove patient benefit
st.an: The study materially strengthens the cluster’s proposition by jointly assessing financial and patient-facing outcomes in the same acquired practices: colonoscopy prices rose after private-equity acquisition, while six measured quality indicators showed no statistically significant improvement. It also reinforces the cluster’s caution by acknowledging limited power for rare complications and observational constraints.
qs: Colonoscopy prices at PE-acquired gastroenterology practices increased by 4.5% (95% CI, 2.5%-6.6%; *P* < .001) relative to independent gastroenterology practices.
No statistically significant associations were detected for the 6 quality measures analyzed.

mo.t: Human-AI decisions: Self-knowledge conditions unrealized gains

kp.k: Private equity acquisition is expanding rapidly in physician services
kp.d: The authors report prior research finding a 6-fold increase in physician-practice acquisitions between 2012 and 2021 and that gastroenterology had the highest share of physicians in PE-owned practices, at 13.1%. They frame potential technological and operational efficiencies against concerns about short-term financial incentives affecting prices, quality and access. These are healthcare claims, not findings about AI or legal services.
qs: A recent study found a 6-fold increase in the number of PE acquisitions of physician practices between 2012 and 2021.

While the influx of capital from PE has the potential to create technological and operational efficiencies, many have feared that PE’s short-term financial incentives may negatively impact health care prices, quality, or access.

kp.k: Study compares acquired practices with consistently independent practices
kp.d: This difference-in-differences economic evaluation used 2012–2021 commercial claims and acquisitions during 2015–2021, providing at least three preacquisition years. The sample comprised 718,851 treated colonoscopies, 590,900 patients, 1,494 physicians and 1,240 acquired sites, versus 637,990 control colonoscopies, 527,380 patients, 2,550 physicians and 2,657 independent sites. Models used physician and year fixed effects, patient characteristics and procedure-code controls; Sun and Abraham estimation addressed staggered acquisition timing and heterogeneous treatment effects.
qs: Only physicians in practices acquired by PE firms from 2015 to 2021 were considered treated so that all treated physicians had a preperiod of at least 3 years (ie, 2012-2014).

The comparison group of physicians included only physicians who were independent throughout the study period, with independent being defined as employed by a practice that was not owned by a corporate entity (eg, a health system).

kp.k: Single-procedure analysis separates price changes from procedure shifting
kp.d: The authors focus on colonoscopies to distinguish higher prices from shifts toward more expensive procedures, which can also raise average allowed amounts per claim. Price includes insurer reimbursement and patient cost-sharing; spending is annual colonoscopy allowed amounts per physician. The study jointly evaluates prices and six claims-based quality measures for the same acquired and control practices.
qs: The average allowed amount per claim would increase if the prices of all (or most) procedures increased, but would also increase if physicians simply shifted to performing more expensive procedures postacquisition.
Price was measured as the allowed amount for the colonoscopy procedure, which includes reimbursement by insurers and any patient cost-sharing.

kp.k: Acquisition was associated with higher colonoscopy prices
kp.d: Prices increased by 4.5% relative to independent practices (95% CI, 2.5%–6.6%; P < .001). Preacquisition price coefficients were near zero and not statistically significant; prices were 4.0% higher in the acquisition year (95% CI, 2.0%–6.0%; P < .001), reaching 7.8% three years afterward (95% CI, 4.9%–10.6%; P < .001). These are observational event-study estimates subject to the authors’ selection and unobserved-confounding limitations.
qs: Colonoscopy prices at PE-acquired gastroenterology practices increased by 4.5% (95% CI, 2.5%-6.6%; *P* < .001) relative to independent gastroenterology practices.
The preperiod coefficient estimates (from 6 to 2 years before) all hover around zero and are not statistically significant.
The estimated price effect reached 7.8% (95% CI, 4.9%-10.6%; *P* < .001) 3 years after acquisition.

kp.k: Higher market shares accompanied larger estimated price increases
kp.d: For acquired practices above the 2021 metropolitan-market-share 75th percentile of 24.4%, the estimated price increase was 6.7% (95% CI, 4.2%–9.3%; P < .001), versus 4.5% overall. The authors explicitly caution that these estimates cannot be established as statistically different. Thus, the subgroup finding does not establish a statistically significant market-share differential.
qs: While the 6.7% estimate is larger than the point estimate of the main price effect, the 95% CIs are wide enough on the estimates that it cannot be determined whether the estimates are statistically different from each other.

kp.k: Spending and utilization increased, but pretrends complicate attribution
kp.d: Estimated spending per physician increased 16.0% (95% CI, 8.4%–24.0%), colonoscopies per physician 12.1% (95% CI, 5.3%–19.4%), and unique patients per physician 11.3% (95% CI, 4.4%–18.5%), all P < .001. At six years after acquisition, corresponding differences reached 50.0%, 48.8% and 43.8%. However, all three measures were already increasing before acquisition, limiting attribution of their subsequent growth to PE ownership.
qs: For all 3 outcome variables, the gap between PE-acquired and control practices grows gradually from the year of acquisition all the way until 6 years postacquisition, the maximum number of years postacquisition observed in the data.
However, these results should be interpreted with caution, as it is clear from each of the graphs that these measures were increasing for the PE-acquired practices prior to acquisition.

kp.k: No statistically significant changes appeared in measured quality
kp.d: The study detected no statistically significant acquisition associations for polypectomy detection, incomplete colonoscopies, cardiovascular complications, serious gastrointestinal complications, nonserious gastrointestinal complications or any complication. Polypectomy served as a claims-observable proxy for adenoma detection. Limited power for rare complications qualifies the null findings; they do not demonstrate that every dimension of quality was unchanged.
qs: No statistically significant associations were detected for the 6 quality measures analyzed.
Because measuring ADR from claims is difficult, we instead use the polypectomy rate, given that it has been shown to correlate well with ADR.
Second, our power to detect changes for rare events for some of our quality measures (eg, perforation, infection) may be limited.

kp.k: Sensitivity analyses preserve direction but alter price-effect magnitude
kp.d: Restricting data to 2012–2019 to exclude pandemic-period influences preserved the main pattern of higher prices, spending and utilization without detected quality changes. Excluding 2015 acquisitions increased the estimated price effect from 4.5% to 10.8% (95% CI, 8.1%–13.4%; P < .001). The authors note that larger gastroenterology acquisitions occurred in or after 2016.
qs: The overall takeaways from the main analysis, higher prices, spending, and utilization with no effect on quality, are the same for the 2012 to 2019 subsample.
Excluding 2015 acquisitions increased the estimated price effect from 4.5% (95% CI, 2.5%-6.6%; *P* < .001) to 10.8% (95% CI, 8.1%-13.4%; *P* < .001).

kp.k: Increased physician throughput may reflect redistributed clinical tasks
kp.d: The authors interpret physician fixed effects as showing that individual gastroenterologists performed more colonoscopies among observed insurers’ enrollees, rather than practice growth reflecting only additional physician hiring. They propose, without testing, that nurse practitioners or physician assistants could screen new consultations and release physician time for procedures. The mechanism remains speculation because how throughput increased was outside the study’s scope.
qs: How gastroenterologists could perform more colonoscopies is beyond the scope of this study, but one possibility is that advanced practice providers (eg, nurse practitioners, physician assistants) screened new consultations, leaving physicians with more time for procedures.

kp.k: Acquisition coverage and selection limit causal interpretation
kp.d: Acquisition identification relied on publicly announced deals, potentially missing smaller acquisitions and biasing estimates toward the null. Practice-data match rates ranged from 70% to 84%, with a weighted mean of 75%; claims were found for 87% of gastroenterologist identifiers. Fixed effects and patient controls could not fully eliminate nonrandom decisions to sell, physician-behavior changes or unobserved time-varying confounding.
qs: First, despite efforts to use and validate comprehensive data on PE firms acquiring physician practices, observed acquisitions were limited to those publicly announced, which can lead to underreporting of small acquisitions, potentially biasing our results toward a null result.
Physicians’ decisions to sell to PE are unlikely to be exogenous.
The inclusion of patient characteristics in our model attempted to alleviate this concern, but it was not a concern we could fully eliminate.

kp.k: Authors recommend monitoring ownership and increasing transaction transparency
kp.d: The authors argue that increased prices and spending without corresponding measured quality gains warrant policy monitoring of PE investment. They situate this recommendation in a spring 2024 federal request for information about corporate healthcare transactions, including deals below the Hart-Scott-Rodino reporting threshold ($126.4 million in 2025). They report that public comments called for proposed-transaction notification and patient notification of ownership changes; 15 states required healthcare merger-and-acquisition notification.
qs: Policymakers may be well advised to monitor PE investment in physician practices given the increase in prices and spending without a commensurate increase in quality.

One theme that emerged was the need for increased transparency, including notification for proposed mergers and acquisitions in health care, which 15 states require, and for patients to be notified of changes in corporate ownership.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Arnold and colleagues report that private equity acquisition of gastroenterology practices was associated with higher colonoscopy prices, spending and utilization, without detectable changes in measured quality.
pts.d: This is a cross-domain health care source, not a source about AI or legal services. The authors report a 4.5% relative price increase, a 16.0% increase in colonoscopy spending per physician, a 12.1% increase in colonoscopies per physician and an 11.3% increase in unique patients per physician. No statistically significant associations were detected for six quality measures. The price estimate for practices with 2021 market shares above 24.4% was 6.7%, although the authors state that this estimate cannot be established as statistically different from the main estimate. They suggest that advanced practice providers screening consultations could free physicians to perform more procedures, but explicitly present this as a possible mechanism outside the study's scope, not a demonstrated finding.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The claims rest on a difference-in-differences event study linking acquisition records, physician characteristics and commercial insurance claims.
pts.d: The authors analyze approximately 1.3 million colonoscopies among more than 1.1 million patients, comparing 1,494 physicians at 1,240 PE-acquired sites with 2,550 physicians at 2,657 independent sites. Acquisition information comes from PitchBook and Irving Levin Associates, physician information from IQVIA, and claims from HCCI. The study uses Sun and Abraham event study estimates to address staggered acquisitions and heterogeneous treatment effects, with physician and year fixed effects and patient and procedure controls. Quality is measured through polypectomy, incomplete colonoscopy and four adverse-event indicators; polypectomy is a claims-observable proxy for adenoma detection. Price preperiod estimates were not statistically significant, but spending and utilization were already increasing before acquisition. The authors acknowledge potentially unobserved acquisitions, limited power for rare complications and unresolved selection or time-varying confounding.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The findings concern acquisitions during 2015–2021, observed through claims from 2012–2021, rather than a forecast.
pts.d: Published in 2025, the study uses an event window extending from six years before to six years after acquisition, with the preceding year as the reference period. Treated physicians must have at least three preacquisition years; controls remain independent throughout the study. The authors report a 4.0% relative price increase in the acquisition year and a 7.8% increase three years later. The high-market-share analysis uses market shares measured in 2021. Restricting data to 2012–2019 preserves the main qualitative conclusions; excluding 2015 acquisitions raises the price estimate to 10.8%. Spending and utilization pretrends qualify attribution of their subsequent increases to acquisition. Absence of statistically significant quality changes is limited to the measures and observation period studied.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The affected groups are commercially insured colonoscopy patients, insurers, gastroenterologists and acquired practices; the authors also identify implications for policymakers.
pts.d: The price measure includes insurer reimbursement and patient cost-sharing, but the study does not separately estimate how the increase is divided between those payers. Physicians at acquired practices perform more colonoscopies per physician, rather than practice-level growth merely reflecting additional hiring. Patients show no detectable improvement in the six measured quality outcomes. Independent practices provide the comparison group, rather than health-system-owned practices. The authors recommend monitoring PE investment and greater transparency about corporate ownership because observed increases in prices and spending lack corresponding measured quality improvements. The results concern the commercial insurance claims population studied, not all patients or all health care services.
